name: Paĩ Tavyterã Guaraní

catalog_quote: El guaraní de este estudio es una lengua acentual yámbica, donde el acento de una palabra o léxico es de intensidad y se marca con mayor prominencia en la sílaba tónica (Hayes 1980; Hyman 1985, 2015; Morales-Front 2014; Chávez-Peón 2015). [p. 181] ... este guaraní es de alineamiento yámbico que empieza de la última sílaba de derecha a izquierda (tabla 1) a nivel de la raíz o base. [p. 182] ... Todos muestran al menos un acento primario (obligatoriedad), el cual recae generalmente en la última sílaba de la palabra (culminatividad), que tiene el grado más alto en prominencia. [p. 183] ... este guaraní es yámbico, con alternancia rítmica direccional de derecha a izquierda con cantidad moraica insensible permitida en sílabas no acentuadas [p. 190] ... El acento primario recae en la última sílaba de la base o raíz, es decir, presenta un sistema acentual yámbico. El alineamiento es de derecha a izquierda. Generalmente hay una alternancia rítmica en bisílabos (fuerte-débil), en trisílabos (fuerte-débil-medio) y en tetrasílabos (aún no determinable), la cual evita así “choques”. Se muestra como una lengua “ligada”. Por lo tanto, la palabra prosódica mínima suele terminar con el acento primario del pie en el extremo derecho de las raíces. [p. 228]
world_status: statement found in an open source

Generalmente hay una alternancia rítmica en bisílabos (fuerte-débil), en trisílabos (fuerte-débil-medio) y en tetrasílabos (aún no determinable), la cual evita así "choques". new_statements.translation: The Guaraní of this study is an iambic stress language, in which the stress of a word or lexeme is one of intensity and is marked by greater prominence on the stressed syllable [...] (p. 181) [...] Primary stress falls on the last syllable of the base or root, i.e. it has an iambic stress system. Alignment is from right to left. There is generally a rhythmic alternation in disyllables (strong-weak), in trisyllables (strong-weak-medium) and in tetrasyllables (not yet determinable), which thus avoids 'clashes'. It shows itself to be a 'bounded' language. Therefore the minimal prosodic word usually ends with the primary stress of the foot at the right edge of roots. (p. 228)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (intensity) stress falls on the final syllable of the lexical root/base; iambic feet built right-to-left give alternating secondary stresses ([ʃi.ˈɾu] 'abuelo', [ˌɨ.sɨ.ˈpo] 'liana', [u.ˌɾu.ta.ˈu] 'Nyctibius griseus'). Prefixes are unstressed; lexical roots, some particles and some suffixes are tonic (e.g. -pa), and a tonic suffix can make the root's stress retract to its penult to avoid clash ([e.ˈɟʝu.hu.ˌpa.ma]). Quantity-insensitive (diphthongs/complex nuclei may be unstressed); a word-final hiatus can carry primary stress on its second vowel ([a.ɾa.ˈi] 'cielo'). Author terms the system 'acento fijo' with a minority of 'libre de acento' items.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: alternating right-to-left from the primary (iambic feet), e.g. [ˌe.ɾe.ˈna] 'dilo', [ˌa.mo.ˈi] 'pongo'; spectrogram shows a 2-1-3 intensity scheme (secondary at word start, weakest syllable adjacent to the primary); in 4-syllable roots the secondary was found on the second syllable (p. 185, 225).
new_statements.exceptions: A subgroup of nominals with penultimate (non-final) stress: ['o.ɣa] 'casa', ['a.ɾa] 'cielo', ['ho.po] 'fleco', [ta.'ʔɨ.ɾa] 'hijo de hombre', ['ho.ko] 'garza', [ha.'vi.a] 'zorzal' (pp. 225-227; 'casa' and 'hijo de hombre' explained diachronically by the PTG final consonant + argumentative -a, the rest unexplained); Spanish loans keep the source language's stress (['ha.ʃa] 'hacha', ['o.ɾa] 'hora', ['ka.ʃo], [ka.'ɾaŋ.ʃio]) (p. 227); a lexical minimal pair kuéra [ˈkŭe.ɾa] 'plural' vs kuera [kŭe.ˈɾa] 'curar' (pp. 184, 191); discourse focus/topicalization and clash-avoidance with tonic suffixes can move the most prominent syllable off the final (p. 186-187).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the root/base (raíz o base) = prosodic word; based on elicited roots (35-50 verb roots, 222 inflected entries, up to 8 syllables) with instrumental (spectrogram) support from 5 speakers of Ita Guasu, Amambay. Phrase-level (frase sintagmática) prosody explicitly left unexplored; alienable monosyllabic roots can produce strong-strong clashes at phrase level.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes the Paĩ Tavyterã Guaraní of the community of Ita Guasu (Amambay, Paraguay), which the author labels 'pãi tavyterã guaraní' = pait1247 (ISO pta). Glottolog files it under pait1247, while most other 'pait1247' references in Glottolog are in fact on Kaiwá of Brazil (kaiw1246, a separate Glottolog language); the thesis's own comparative tables treat Kaiowá as a sister variety. The earlier scan's 'the named source could not be reached' classification is superseded: the named source is open access at the CIESAS repository.
